title: QWERTY’s Secret
sub: Grades 3–4 · Why the letters on a keyboard are where they are
objective: Students will discover why the letters on a keyboard are where they are: in 1868 Sholes’ typewriter jammed when typists went too fast, and in the best-known account he split up letters that often go together. They will separate the myth from the fact, and explain why we still type on his pattern.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The keyboard you use every day was shaped by a problem with a machine 150 years old. Things are often the way they are for a reason, and finding the reason is what historians and inventors do.

items.text: explain the problem Sholes had: metal arms that jammed when typists went too fast
items.question: explain why Sholes’ typewriter jammed?

items.text: describe how, in the best-known account, his keyboard split up letter pairs like TH and HE
items.question: say how the keyboard split up letter pairs?

items.text: tell the myth about QWERTY from the fact
items.question: tell the myth from the fact?

items.text: explain why we still type on QWERTY, long after the jamming was solved
items.question: explain why we still use QWERTY today?

materials: The Typing Station on a screen, open at its *Top row* tab
Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed
A keyboard or a phone, if you have one to pass around
connection: **Online,** the Typing Station’s *Top row* tab checks the letters of any word; try the bottom row too. **In the exhibition,** read *QWERTY’s Accidental Empire* and look at the Urania’s keys.

steps.title: Not in ABC order
script: Show the top row of the keyboard on page 3, or pass round a keyboard. Read the letters aloud together: Q, W, E, R, T, Y… *“Why aren’t the letters in ABC order? Wouldn’t ABC be easier to learn?”* Write a few guesses on the board. Then: *“The answer is a secret 150 years old. It starts with a problem.”*

screen.text: Q  W  E  R  T  Y  U  I  O  P

steps.purpose: Start from something students use every day and have never questioned.
students: Read the top row of a keyboard.
Why aren’t the letters in ABC order?

steps.title: Jammed!
script: **The problem.** Read the poster aloud: *“In 1868, Christopher Latham Sholes, a Milwaukee newspaper editor, was perfecting his "Type-Writer" machine when he encountered a frustrating problem: when typists worked too quickly, the metal arms carrying the letters would jam together.”* Show the Urania on page 3: each key works a metal arm, a typebar, that swings up to the paper.

screen.alt: A black Urania portable typewriter seen from the front: four rows of round silver-rimmed keys, the name Urania in gold above them and Clemens Müller A.G. Dresden in gold along the base
screen.caption: The Urania typewriter from the posters: behind the keys, the curve of metal typebars

steps.purpose: See the machine and understand its problem: fast fingers made the typebars jam.
students: Find the curve of metal arms behind the keys.
What would happen if two swung up at once?

steps.title: Split up the pairs
script: **The solution.** *“His solution, in the best-known account, was ingenious—he analyzed letter frequency in the English language and separated commonly paired letters like "TH" and "HE" across the keyboard.”* Find T, H and E on the keyboard together. The poster adds: *“This seemingly random arrangement, which placed "QWERTY" across the top row, actually prevented mechanical collisions.”* Point out *in the best-known account*: the exhibition is careful to say this is the story most often told.
steps.purpose: Find the solution on the keyboard itself: common pairs set apart.
students: Find T and H on the keyboard. Are they side by side?

steps.title: Myth or fact?
script: **The myth.** Put the statement on the screen and vote. Then read: *“Contrary to popular myth, Sholes didn't design QWERTY to slow typists down—he designed it to let them type as fast as possible without breaking the machine.”* Finally: *“By the time electric typewriters eliminated the jamming problem, QWERTY had already conquered the world.”* Millions had trained their muscle memory on this layout, and entire industries depended on it. In our age of touchscreens and voice recognition, we still arrange virtual keyboards in Sholes' pattern—even though there are no physical keys to jam.

screen.text: Sholes designed QWERTY to slow typists down.

steps.purpose: Use the source to bust a myth, then ask why the pattern stayed.
students: Myth or fact? Vote with a thumb.
If the jamming was solved, why do we still use QWERTY?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three find the split pairs, bust the myth and hunt for words that use only the top row.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Color the top row and find T, H and E. Sort four statements into myth and fact, check six words for top-row letters, and say why we still use QWERTY.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Put the story in a cause-and-effect chain, count TH and HE in a poster sentence, bust the myth with evidence, and hunt for the longest top-row word.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Solve the bottom-row puzzle, judge the Dvorak keyboard’s test, explain why QWERTY survived, and look closely at the Urania’s own keys.

steps.purpose: Investigate the keyboard independently, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three find the letter pairs, bust the myth and hunt for top-row words.

steps.title: Beat ten
script: The poster says *“typewriter”* remains one of the longest words you can type using only the top row. It has ten letters. Ask for the longest top-row words students found, and check each letter together. On the Typing Station’s *Top row* tab, type them in and *Post the list to the board*.
steps.purpose: Share the top-row hunt: the poster’s own word has ten letters. Can anyone beat it?
students: Check every letter: is it on the top row?

steps.title: Look back
script: Then ask the objectives back, from the screen or page 1: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask a Red Level reader to answer the last one.

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.
